qs.q: A clinical clerk is summarizing breast pathology risk categories for an upcoming exam. Which matched pairing of lesion category and lifetime cancer risk is entirely accurate according to standard data?
o: A. Nonproliferative changes — lifetime risk about 25 to 30 percent
B. Proliferative without atypia — lifetime risk about 13 to 17 percent
D. Carcinoma in situ — lifetime risk about 5 to 7 percent
C. Proliferative with atypia — lifetime risk about 13 to 17 percent
qs.e: Proliferative disease with atypia carries a lifetime cancer risk of about 13 to 17 percent (4 to 5x risk). Nonproliferative changes have a risk matching the general population (~3%), proliferative without atypia is ~5 to 7 percent, and carcinoma in situ is ~25 to 30 percent.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Breast pathology covers benign and malignant lesions, focusing on clinical presentation, diagnostic workup, and management. Clinicians learn to integrate history, imaging, and pathology to guide treatment and follow‑up.

sections.p: Breast pathology refers to any abnormal tissue change in the breast, from cysts to invasive cancers. Diagnosis combines clinical exam, imaging, and histology.
b: Malignant: ductal carcinoma in situ, invasive carcinoma

t.b: Detects masses or calcifications; abnormal findings suggest biopsy.
Characterises cystic vs solid lesions; guides needle biopsy.
Provides tissue for histology and immunohistochemistry; confirms diagnosis.
Determines hormone receptor status; guides targeted therapy.

sections.p: Staging uses the TNM system, assessing tumour size (T), nodal spread (N), and metastasis (M). Staging informs prognosis and treatment choice.
Risk factors vary by age and ethnicity. The most common causes of breast cancer are hormonal exposure, genetics, and lifestyle.
b: Hormonal: early menarche, late menopause, hormone replacement therapy

sections.p: Patients may notice a lump, skin dimpling, nipple discharge, or pain. Benign lesions often present as painless, mobile masses.
Workup starts with imaging, followed by tissue sampling and receptor testing. In low‑resource settings, clinical assessment and basic imaging guide management.

t.b: Screening for asymptomatic women; detects calcifications.
First‑line imaging when mammogram unavailable; evaluates cystic nature.
Rapid cytology when core biopsy not feasible; limited for definitive diagnosis.
Assesses ER, PR, HER2; essential for treatment planning.

sections.p: Urgent signs include rapid growth, ulceration, or systemic symptoms. Complications can be local (infections) or distant (metastasis).
Treatment targets the underlying lesion and its biology. Surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy are tailored to stage and receptor status.
b: Lumpectomy or mastectomy for localized disease
Hormonal therapy for ER/PR positive tumors
Targeted therapy for HER2 positive tumors

t.b: Blocks estrogen receptors; used in ER+ early breast cancer.
Inhibits aromatase; preferred in postmenopausal women with ER+ disease.
Targets HER2; combined with chemotherapy improves survival.

sections.p: Surveillance includes regular exams and imaging. Prevention focuses on modifiable risk factors and genetic counselling.
b: Lifestyle changes: diet, exercise, limit alcohol

t.b: Identifies BRCA mutations; informs surveillance and prophylactic surgery.

sections.p: Benign breast disease can mimic cancer clinically and radiologically.
b: Intraductal papilloma vs. ductal carcinoma in situ

sections.p: Certain tests may yield false negatives or positives, especially in dense breast tissue or low‑resource settings.
b: Mammogram sensitivity lower in dense breasts
Fine‑needle aspiration may miss invasive components
HER2 testing requires adequate tissue quality

faq.q: What is the most common type of breast cancer?
faq.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most frequent.

faq.q: Can a breast lump be cancer?
faq.a: Yes, but many lumps are benign; imaging and biopsy confirm.

faq.q: Why is hormone receptor status important?
faq.a: It determines eligibility for targeted hormonal or HER2 therapies.
